--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Leadership and the Project Manager ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Distinguish** leadership from management in a project context. 2. **Explain** the four foundations of a project partnership and Bennis's four competencies of the "new project leader." 3. **Match** a leadership style (command & control, relating, democratic, hands-on, coaching) to a team situation, and state each style's downside. 4. **Score** a leadership self-assessment and interpret the result. 5. **Describe** the stages of team development and what the leader does in each. 6. **Apply** motivation theory --- Maslow, Herzberg, and expectancy --- to diagnose a performance problem. 7. **Identify** the five components of emotional intelligence and why they matter to a project leader.
Before we begin: recall a team you would follow anywhere Who led it, and what did they *do* --- not what title they held? Most people describe behaviour, not authority. That is the whole chapter in one observation.
## Introduction: the project manager as mini-CEO Leading the RC-vehicle project means more than tracking a Gantt chart. The brief has your team learning a **new assembly line** with a real learning curve, working with an **unproven supplier**, and racing a **holiday deadline**. The PM *"encapsulates the role of a mini-CEO"* --- expected to manage holistically from start to finish: acquiring resources, motivating and building the team, holding a vision *and* fighting fires, and communicating relentlessly. *"A PM cannot get up in the morning and think 'I don't want to communicate today.'"* ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** On an automotive launch, the line lead who can only give orders stalls the moment a novel problem appears; the one who has built a team that raises issues early hits the job-one date. In food processing, a sanitation crew that understands *why* the changeover procedure matters follows it at 3 a.m. when no one is watching. Leadership is what fills the gap between the procedure and reality. :::
## Leadership versus management **Leadership** is *the ability to inspire confidence and support among the people needed to achieve organizational goals.* A **manager** holds a title that lets them *plan, organize, direct, and control* others. Leadership may be part of the manager's job, but the other roles are more administrative. Leaders create a sense of **partnership**. Four things build it: | Foundation | What it means | |---|---| | **Exchange of purpose** | Every member knows the project's goals and vision. | | **A right to say "no"** | Members can voice professional disagreement. *Losing an argument is acceptable; losing the right to disagree is not.* | | **Joint accountability** | Every member owns the project's outcomes --- good or bad. | | **Absolute honesty** | All information becomes community information. | ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Manager and leader emphases. Neither column is 'bad' --- a project manager needs both, but leans on the right-hand behaviours during execution.](04-Leadership-and-the-Project-Manager_files/figure-html/fig-leader-vs-manager-04-1.png){#fig-leader-vs-manager-04 fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### Bennis's four competencies of the new project leader 1. **The power of appreciation** --- recognize and reward others' talent; your job is not to outshine the team but to let it develop. 2. **Keep reminding people what's important** --- amid the noise of problems, keep everyone's eye on the prize. 3. **Generate and sustain trust** --- through authenticity, fairness, honesty, and caring. Honesty is the trait people look for most. 4. **The leader and the led are intimate allies** --- leadership supports the team's effort; it does not dominate it. ## The five leadership styles Effective PMs switch styles to fit the person and the situation. | Style | Use it when | The downside if overused | |---|---|---| | **Command & control** | You know the best way and the other person doesn't; beginners; a crisis | Team feels devalued; learned helplessness; kills creativity and initiative | | **Relating** | Building rapport, bonding the team, focusing people on common goals | Can't make tough calls or take charge in a crisis; seen as weak | | **Democratic** | *Planning* --- getting buy-in and reality-based plans from those who will execute | *Execution* often needs autocracy; consensus-building wastes a critical deadline | | **Hands-on** | You must step in and model the way to get a stuck task done | Disempowering; low morale; you become the bottleneck | | **Coaching** | Long-term development; asking questions that lead people to their own solutions | Slow for short-term objectives --- but it is the style most managers most need to build | ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Situational leadership: match the style to how ready the team is. New or struggling teams need direction; capable, committed teams need delegation.](04-Leadership-and-the-Project-Manager_files/figure-html/fig-situational-04-1.png){#fig-situational-04 fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ### Try it yourself: pick the style ```{=html}
``` ### Try it yourself: which quadrant is this team member in? Rate the person's **competence** on the specific task and their **commitment** to doing it, both 0--1, and the situational-leadership quadrant above follows directly. Live cell --- try Owen from the case study below, then a veteran who is skilled but burning out. ```{=html}

Situational Leadership Calculator

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: situational-quadrant-04 team_member <- "Owen (co-op student, mounting-tab idea)" competence <- 0.3 # 0-1: skill/experience on this specific task commitment <- 0.8 # 0-1: confidence and motivation to do it # Readiness model: a newcomer who is keen but unskilled needs direction; # one who is losing confidence as the work gets hard needs coaching. style <- if (competence < 0.5 && commitment >= 0.5) { "Directing (high direction, low support)" } else if (competence < 0.5 && commitment < 0.5) { "Coaching (high direction, high support)" } else if (competence >= 0.5 && commitment < 0.5) { "Supporting (low direction, high support)" } else { "Delegating (low direction, low support)" } par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Competence on this task", ylab = "Commitment", main = "Situational leadership quadrant") abline(v = 0.5, h = 0.5, col = "#bdc3c7", lwd = 2) text(c(0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 0.75), c(0.25, 0.75, 0.25, 0.75), labels = c("Coaching", "Directing", "Supporting", "Delegating"), col = "#7f8c8d", cex = 1.3) points(competence, commitment, pch = 19, cex = 3, col = "#e74c3c") cat(sprintf("Recommended style: %s\n", style)) cat(sprintf("Team member %s\n", team_member)) cat(sprintf("Competence %.1f\n", competence)) cat(sprintf("Commitment %.1f\n", commitment)) ```
### Try it yourself: the leadership self-assessment The course quiz has 18 statements rated 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Items **1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16** sum to a **command & control** score; items **2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17** to a **democratic** score; items **3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18** to a **relating** score. Enter your 18 answers and run. ```{webr-r} #| label: leadership-score-04 # Replace with your own 1-5 answers to items 1..18, in order: responses <- c(2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, # items 1-6 2, 4, 4, 2, 4, 4, # items 7-12 2, 5, 2, 2, 4, 3) # items 13-18 cc <- sum(responses[c(1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16)]) dem <- sum(responses[c(2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17)]) rel <- sum(responses[c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18)]) scores <- c("Command & Control" = cc, "Democratic" = dem, "Relating" = rel) for (nm in names(scores)) cat(sprintf("%-18s %2d / 30\n", nm, scores[nm])) cat(sprintf("\nYour dominant style: %s\n", names(which.max(scores)))) cat("Remember: the best PMs deliberately use all three depending on the situation.\n") ``` ## Building the team Teams develop through predictable stages, and the leader's job changes with each: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Team performance through Tuckman's stages. Performance dips during storming before rising; a leader who expects the dip manages it instead of panicking.](04-Leadership-and-the-Project-Manager_files/figure-html/fig-tuckman-04-1.png){#fig-tuckman-04 fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: - **Forming** --- polite, uncertain. Leader: **direct** --- clarify goals, roles, the charter. - **Storming** --- conflict over approach and authority; performance dips. Leader: **coach** --- surface conflict, don't suppress it. - **Norming** --- norms settle, trust builds. Leader: **support**. - **Performing** --- the team runs itself. Leader: **delegate**. - **Adjourning** --- the project ends; recognize contributions and manage the transition (see [Chapter 13](13-Project-Closeout-and-Termination.qmd)). ### Try it yourself: which stage is the team in? ```{=html}
``` ## Motivating the team ### Worked Example 1: Herzberg --- is this a hygiene problem or a motivator problem? Herzberg splits job factors into **hygiene factors** (pay, conditions, policy, supervision --- their *absence* causes dissatisfaction, but their presence does not motivate) and **motivators** (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, growth --- these drive engagement). Live cell --- re-classify the complaints, or add your own, and see which get fixed first. ```{webr-r} #| label: herzberg-example-04 complaints <- data.frame( issue = c("Cramped, hot project room", "No recognition for hitting the drop-test milestone", "Confusing expense policy", "Same repetitive CAD cleanup every week", "Parking is far from the building"), type = c("Hygiene", "Motivator", "Hygiene", "Motivator", "Hygiene") ) print(complaints, row.names = FALSE) fix_first <- complaints$issue[complaints$type == "Hygiene"] cat("\nFix the hygiene issues to stop dissatisfaction:\n - ", paste(fix_first, collapse = "\n - "), "\n", sep = "") cat("\nThen add motivators (recognition, varied/owned work) to actually raise engagement.\n") ``` ### Try it yourself: hygiene or motivator? ```{=html}
``` ### Try it yourself: expectancy theory Vroom's expectancy model says motivation is the product of three beliefs, each 0--1: **Expectancy** (effort → performance), **Instrumentality** (performance → reward), and **Valence** (how much the person wants the reward). $$\text{Motivation} = E \times I \times V$$ Because it is a product, **any factor near zero kills motivation**. ```{webr-r} #| label: expectancy-04 team_member <- data.frame( name = c("Priya", "Sam", "Dev"), expectancy = c(0.9, 0.8, 0.4), # "if I try, I can hit the target" instrumentality = c(0.8, 0.3, 0.9), # "hitting it gets me the reward" valence = c(0.7, 0.9, 0.8) # "I want that reward" ) team_member$motivation <- with(team_member, expectancy * instrumentality * valence) print(team_member, row.names = FALSE) weakest <- team_member$name[which.min(team_member$motivation)] cat(sprintf("\nLowest motivation: %s\n", weakest)) cat("Look at which of E, I, V is dragging the product down -- that is where the leader intervenes.\n") cat("(Sam doesn't believe performance leads to the reward; Dev doesn't believe he can hit the target.)\n") ``` ### Try it yourself: expectancy by hand Compute each person's motivation as E x I x V, then find who is least motivated. Each team picks its own **data set**. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution Multiply the three factors for each person. In data set 1, Cal's motivation is 0.8 x 0.2 x 0.9 = 0.144: instrumentality is the weak factor, so the leader's job is to make the link from performance to reward visible. Because the model is a product, one factor near zero drags the whole score down.
## Emotional intelligence Goleman: *the most effective leaders all have a high degree of emotional intelligence* --- IQ and technical skill are just the entry ticket. Five components: - **Self-awareness** --- a clear view of your strengths, weaknesses, drives, and ego needs. - **Self-regulation** --- keeping yourself under control; think before you act. - **Motivation** --- driven to your own potential *and* to drawing the best from each team member. - **Empathy** --- weighing team members' feelings when making a decision. - **Social skill** --- managing relationships with purpose. ## Key Takeaways - **Management** administers systems; **leadership** inspires people. A PM needs both and leans on leadership during execution. - Partnership rests on **exchange of purpose, the right to say no, joint accountability, and absolute honesty**. Bennis: **appreciate, remind what matters, build trust, be an ally.** - Switch among the **five styles** --- command & control, relating, democratic, hands-on, coaching --- by situation. Plan democratically; often execute autocratically. Every style overused has a cost. - Teams move through **forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning**; performance dips in storming --- expect it and coach through it. - Diagnose motivation with **Herzberg** (fix hygiene to stop dissatisfaction, add motivators to raise engagement) and **expectancy** ($E \times I \times V$ --- any factor near zero kills it). - **Emotional intelligence** --- self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skill --- separates effective project leaders from merely competent ones. ## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 4 ::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 4: The Whiteboard Moment"} Four weeks into the Meridian Trailblazer prototype, the team gathers for its regular Tuesday design review --- Priya Nandakumar (tooling), Marcus Webb (procurement), Sofia Reyes (quality and test), and Owen Matsuda, a co-op student newly rotated in to shadow the tooling work. The charter Daniel Cho signed in Week 3 is in hand, the aluminium body-and-frame decision from Week 1 is locked, and the team has moved on to something less settled: which motor and controller supplier to commit to, MCS or the newer Paragon. It is still an early, informal debate --- no quotes on the table yet --- but it is already loud. Marcus keeps steering the conversation toward Paragon's lower sticker price; Sofia keeps pulling it back to qualification risk. Positions are hardening, side conversations are breaking out, and twice now someone has cut off someone else mid-sentence. You recognize it the moment it starts: this is Tuckman's storming, arriving right on schedule. It is uncomfortable, but it is not a sign anything has gone wrong --- yet. Into that tension, Owen raises a hand and offers an idea about the frame's mounting-tab geometry, something he saw work on a project during a previous rotation. Priya, mid-argument with Marcus and not really listening, cuts him off --- "that's not how we do it here" --- and moves straight back to the supplier debate. The room goes quiet for a beat. The mounting-tab idea was not the real loss; what a new team member just learned is that raising a suggestion here costs something. You do not correct it in the room. You address it afterward, with each person separately, because the two problems call for two different tools. With Owen, you use a coaching style: you ask him to walk you through the mounting-tab idea in full, help him sharpen it into two concrete questions, and set aside five minutes at the next stand-up for him to raise it himself, in front of the team. With Priya, whose tooling judgment has been sound since the Week 1 material call and who does not need you supervising her every interaction, you use a delegating style: a short, low-drama flag that new voices need room to speak in these early weeks, then trust her to follow up with Owen in her own way. Neither conversation is a lecture. Both are sized to how ready each person already is --- direction for the newcomer still finding his footing, room for the veteran who already knows how to lead. ::: ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Pick the style Which leadership style fits each moment on the RC-vehicle project? 1. Kicking off planning for the WBS with the whole team. 2. A moulding press fails at 2 a.m. and the launch date is at risk. 3. A capable senior designer is bored and thinking of leaving. 4. A brand-new co-op student has never used the company's PLM system. 5. The team has gelled and is hitting milestones on its own.
Answers 1. **Democratic** (buy-in, reality-based plan). 2. **Command & control** (crisis; take charge). 3. **Coaching** (long-term development; varied, owned work). 4. **Command & control** initially, moving to **coaching**. 5. **Delegating / supporting** --- stay out of the way.
Problem 2: Expectancy diagnosis A skilled technician has stopped putting in effort on validation testing. In a one-on-one you learn they are certain the extra effort won't change the delivery date because "purchasing will be late anyway." Which expectancy factor is broken, and what do you do?
Answer **Instrumentality** --- they no longer believe performance leads to the outcome. Restoring it means making the link visible again: show how the test results actually gate the next milestone, remove the purchasing blocker or re-sequence around it, and close the loop when their work does move the date.
Problem 3 (discussion): the hands-on trap You are the strongest CAD modeller on the team, and every time someone struggles you take the model over and finish it yourself. The work gets done and is high-quality. Why is this a leadership failure, and what should you do instead?
Discussion points Taking over is the **hands-on** style overused: it is disempowering, tanks morale, stops people learning, and makes you the bottleneck --- the project's throughput is now capped by your personal hours. The **coaching** move is to ask questions that lead the person to the fix, sit with them while they do it, and follow up --- slower once, faster forever.
